title: Smoked Haddock with Poached Egg
subtitle: Milk-poached smoked haddock finished with a soft-set egg
excerpt: Smoked haddock poached in milk becomes remarkably gentle, the smoke softens, the flesh stays moist, and the liquid left in the pan makes a simple sauce. A soft poached egg on top turns it into a proper breakfast.
sourceNotes: Milk-poached smoked haddock with a poached egg is a classic Scottish and northern English breakfast dish, closely related to kedgeree and Arbroath smokie traditions. The milk-poaching method is standard in British cookery.

glossaryTerms.definition: To cook food gently submerged in liquid that is kept just below a simmer, small bubbles rising from the base of the pan but no rolling boil. Used for fish, eggs, and fruit. The gentle heat preserves texture and prevents the food from breaking apart.

content.text: in milk is a quieter version of itself, the smoke mellows, the flesh stays moist and flaking, and the milky cooking liquid becomes a light sauce with almost no effort. A soft poached egg placed on top at serving adds richness and makes the plate feel complete. The two techniques, milk-poaching and egg-poaching, run almost simultaneously once you have the timing right.

Use undyed smoked haddock rather than the bright yellow dyed variety. Undyed fish is a pale cream or ivory colour, it has a cleaner flavour and a better texture. Naturally smoked haddock from a good fishmonger is the ideal, but supermarket undyed haddock works well. Finnan haddie (cold-smoked on the bone from Scotland) is exceptional if you can find it. Avoid vacuum-packed dyed haddock for this dish, the colour comes from artificial colouring, and the flavour is sharper than you want.

Place the {{smoked-haddock}} smoked haddock portions skin-side down in a wide saucepan. Pour over the {{whole-milk}} whole milk, it should come about halfway up the fish. Add a good grinding of {{black-pepper}} black pepper. Bring to the gentlest simmer over a medium-low heat, then reduce to low and cook for eight to ten minutes, depending on thickness. The fish is done when it flakes easily when pressed with a finger, the flesh will separate into large, moist flakes and lose its translucent look. Lift out with a fish slice, leaving the milk in the pan. Add the {{unsalted-butter}} butter to the milk and let it melt; this is your sauce. Keep the fish warm while you cook the eggs.

Bring a separate pan of water to a gentle simmer, enough water to submerge the eggs but not boiling hard. A splash of white wine vinegar helps the white hold together. Crack each {{eggs}} egg into a small cup, then lower the cup to the surface of the water and tip the egg in gently. Poach for three minutes for a set white and a soft, runny yolk. Lift out with a slotted spoon and rest briefly on a folded piece of kitchen paper to drain.

Place each portion of haddock on a thick slice of toast or a bed of wilted spinach. Spoon a little of the buttery milk over the fish. Set the poached egg on top. Scatter over the {{chives}} chives and add a little extra black pepper. The yolk, when you break it, runs into the milk sauce and the fish flakes, it is a dish that rewards eating unhurriedly.

The fish takes about ten minutes and the eggs take three. Start the fish first, get your toast on or wilt your spinach, then drop the eggs in the water with two to three minutes left on the fish. They finish at the same moment. The milk sauce only needs thirty seconds of attention after the fish comes out, keep everything moving and it all comes together at once.

Milk is boiling and curdling in the pan: the heat is too high. The milk must stay at a bare simmer throughout, small bubbles at the edge, nothing more. Reduce the heat as soon as you see it start to tremble.

Poached egg white is ragged and spreading: the eggs are not fresh enough (older eggs have looser whites) or the water is boiling too hard. Use the freshest eggs you have and keep the water at a gentle simmer, not a rolling boil.
Fish is breaking apart in the pan: it was overcooked or moved around too much. Leave it undisturbed while it poaches and lift it out in one piece with a wide fish slice.
